sections.heading: What is on this page is what the platform can provision
sections.body: Regions, operating system versions, control panels and machine sizes are configuration, not marketing copy. The platform lists exactly what a given deployment is configured to offer, and a service that is not configured is shown as unavailable rather than sold and then apologised for.

faqs.q: What is the difference between VPS, public cloud and private cloud?
faqs.a: A VPS is a fixed slice of a shared machine with guaranteed resources. Public cloud is elastic compute that can be resized. Private cloud is capacity reserved for one tenant, so nothing you run shares hardware with anyone else.

faqs.q: Which operating systems can I install?
faqs.a: The operating system catalogue page lists the families and versions the platform is configured to provision. It reflects configuration rather than a list of everything that technically exists.

faqs.q: Do servers include backups?
faqs.a: Backups are a separate, explicitly scheduled job. Some plans include a backup allocation; where they do not, backups can be added to the service.

pages.title: Public Cloud
pages.description: Elastic public cloud instances from CloudHost247: resize compute as demand changes, with the OS catalogue, network controls and monitoring included.

hero.heading: Compute that changes size when your traffic does
hero.lede: Public cloud instances on shared, managed infrastructure — sized for the workload you have today, resizable when it is not enough.

items.title: Resize without rebuilding
items.body: Move to a larger or smaller instance shape as the workload changes, rather than migrating to a new product.

items.title: Fast provisioning
items.body: Instances are created from a configured image, so a working server exists in minutes rather than days.

items.title: Your choice of operating system
items.body: Provision from the catalogue of operating systems the platform holds images for.

items.title: Network control
items.body: Firewall rules and private addressing so the instance is only reachable where it should be.

items.title: Persistence
items.body: Attached storage survives a rebuild of the instance, which is what makes resizing safe.

items.title: Monitoring built in
items.body: Resource telemetry is collected so capacity decisions are made from data rather than from an alert at 03:00.

sections.heading: Region availability is configuration, not a claim
sections.body: A public cloud instance can only be created where the platform has a provider configured for it. The regions list on this deployment shows what is genuinely available; where it is empty, no region is configured and no instance can be promised.

faqs.q: Is public cloud the same as a VPS?
faqs.a: They overlap. The practical difference is elasticity: a VPS is a fixed allocation, while public cloud instances are designed to be resized as demand changes.

faqs.q: Can I control the network at the instance level?
faqs.a: Yes. Firewall rules apply per server, and the platform records the addresses assigned to your service.

faqs.q: Can I run more than one instance?
faqs.a: Yes. Multiple servers can be provisioned and managed from the same account, each with its own operating system and configuration.

pages.title: Private Cloud
pages.description: Private cloud from CloudHost247: isolated compute capacity reserved for one tenant, for workloads that cannot share hardware with anyone else.

hero.heading: Capacity that belongs to one tenant only
hero.lede: Where a workload must not share a machine with anyone else, private cloud gives reserved resources and a defined boundary around them.

items.title: No noisy neighbours
items.body: Performance is not affected by another tenant's load, because there is no other tenant on the same resources.

items.title: A smaller blast radius
items.body: Isolation is a security property as well as a performance one: there is no shared host to be reached through.

items.title: Easier to explain
items.body: A defined boundary is far easier to describe in a compliance or customer questionnaire than shared hosting is.

items.title: Your stack
items.body: Choose the operating system and configuration the workload needs, rather than working around a fixed image.

items.title: Network under your control
items.body: Addressing, firewall rules and connectivity designed around the application.

items.title: Managed if you want it
items.body: Operate it yourself, or have the CloudHost247 team run the platform layer for you.

sections.heading: Private cloud is scoped, not self-service
sections.body: Because the boundary has to be designed — capacity, region, network and operating system — private cloud is quoted against your requirement rather than sold from a fixed price list. The order flow starts with a conversation.

faqs.q: How is this different from a dedicated server?
faqs.a: A dedicated server gives you one physical machine. Private cloud gives you reserved capacity that can be split across instances, with the boundary defined around your organisation.

faqs.q: Can I connect it to my office network?
faqs.a: Connectivity options depend on the facility and the provider configured for the region. Raise the requirement with sales and the available options are confirmed in writing.

faqs.q: Is it multi-tenant under the hood?
faqs.a: It is designed so that your workloads do not share resources with another customer's. The exact architecture depends on the provider and facility involved, and is documented for you before you commit.

pages.title: Enterprise Servers
pages.description: Enterprise-grade server configurations from CloudHost247 for high-capacity workloads, with redundancy options, managed operations and provider-backed hardware.

hero.heading: When a standard server is not enough
hero.lede: High-core, high-memory configurations for databases, virtualisation hosts and platforms that other services depend on — with the operational support to keep them running.

items.title: Sized to the workload
items.body: Configurations are chosen around measured requirements — core count, memory, storage throughput — rather than a fixed tier.

items.title: Built for data-heavy services
items.body: The configuration that makes a database host viable: fast storage, memory for working sets, and cores for concurrency.

items.title: A platform under other services
items.body: When a host runs virtualisation or containers, its failure footprint is larger — so resilience is designed in.

items.title: Monitored as critical
items.body: Telemetry, alerting and capacity tracking so limits are seen before they become incidents.

items.title: Managed operations
items.body: Patch management, hardening and hands-on administration available as part of the service.

items.title: Backups and recovery
items.body: Backup jobs sized to the data volume, with a restore plan that has been agreed rather than improvised.

sections.heading: Quoted against requirements, not published as a price
sections.body: Enterprise configurations depend on hardware availability, redundancy choices and region. Rather than publishing a price that cannot be honoured, enterprise servers are quoted against the requirement you describe.

faqs.q: Do you offer redundant power and networking?
faqs.a: Facility-level redundancy depends on the provider and region. The available options are confirmed per configuration before ordering.

faqs.q: Can you monitor a cluster rather than one server?
faqs.a: Yes. Multiple servers can be monitored from the same account, and the platform records telemetry per service.

faqs.q: Is there a managed option?
faqs.a: Yes. Managed services cover the platform layer — patching, hardening, monitoring response and administration — alongside the server itself.

pages.title: Game Servers
pages.description: Low-latency game server hosting from CloudHost247 with the compute to hold a community, DDoS-path filtering and full administrative access.

hero.heading: Low latency, high uptime, full access
hero.lede: Game servers live or die on two numbers: latency and whether the machine is up. Both come from infrastructure, not from a control panel skin.

items.title: Latency first
items.body: Placement and network path matter more than raw clock speed. The region is chosen to sit near the players.

items.title: Protection against floods
items.body: Game servers are a favourite target for traffic floods. Network-level filtering is part of the service, not an upsell.

items.title: Full access
items.body: Root or administrator access, so you install and configure the game stack the way the community expects.

items.title: Compute that holds a population
items.body: Player counts, plugins and world size drive requirements. Configurations are sized for the community you actually run.

items.title: World data protected
items.body: Scheduled backups of the game data, because a corrupted world file is an unrecoverable community.

items.title: Monitored
items.body: Telemetry on CPU, memory and network so a growth problem shows up before players notice it.

faqs.q: Do you offer a one-click game panel?
faqs.a: The platform provisions servers with the operating system and access you need. Where a specific game panel or a set of preconfigured game templates is not configured in your deployment, that is stated rather than implied.

faqs.q: Which games are supported?
faqs.a: The server is general compute with full access, so it is not limited to a whitelist of games. What matters is the resources the game server needs — tell us and we size for it.

faqs.q: Is DDoS protection included?
faqs.a: Network-level filtering and abuse mitigation are part of the platform. The specific capacity of that mitigation depends on the region and provider.

pages.title: Infrastructure
pages.description: How CloudHost247 infrastructure is organised: providers, regions, network, storage and the operational layer that runs customer services.

hero.heading: The platform under the products
hero.lede: CloudHost247 runs customer services across facilities operated by infrastructure providers, with a control layer that owns provisioning, monitoring, DNS, certificates and backups.

items.title: Facilities and providers
items.body: Compute and network are delivered from data centres operated by infrastructure providers, chosen per region and recorded in the platform.

items.title: Network
items.body: Public addressing, firewalling and private networking sit between the facility and your service, configured per server.

items.title: Control layer
items.body: Provisioning, operating-system images, DNS, certificates, backups and monitoring are owned by the platform rather than by hand.

items.title: Reconciliation
items.body: The platform continuously compares what it believes is provisioned against what the provider reports, so drift is detected rather than discovered.

items.title: Observability
items.body: Server telemetry, service state and operation logs feed the same account view you use.

items.title: Isolation
items.body: Services are separated at the platform layer, and access to provider credentials is restricted and audited.

sections.heading: What this page will not tell you

items.label: A list of cities
items.body: Regions exist only when a provider is configured for them. The data centres page shows what is genuinely configured in your deployment — no decorative world map.

items.label: An uptime percentage
items.body: A published percentage that does not come from measured, customer-visible monitoring would be a number we invented. Service status shows what the platform can verify right now.

items.label: Certifications we do not hold
items.body: Certification claims require an audit report with a name and a date. We publish none we cannot produce.

faqs.q: Where are CloudHost247 servers located?
faqs.a: In the regions configured for your deployment of the platform, which are listed on the data centres page. That list is generated from configuration, so it cannot drift from reality.

faqs.q: Who operates the data centres?
faqs.a: The facilities are operated by infrastructure providers. CloudHost247 operates the platform layer: provisioning, network configuration, monitoring, security response and support.

faqs.q: Can I choose a specific region?
faqs.a: Where more than one region is configured, yes — region is a selection at provisioning time and is recorded on the service.

pages.title: Data Centers
pages.description: The data centre regions CloudHost247 is configured to deploy into, listed from live configuration rather than a marketing map.

hero.heading: Regions we can actually deploy into
hero.lede: This page lists the regions configured for this deployment of the platform. If a region is not configured, it is not offered — which is the only honest way to publish a locations page.

sections.heading: Regions configured on this deployment
sections.emptyMessage: No regions are configured on this deployment yet, so no location is being claimed. Once an administrator configures a provider region it appears here automatically.

items.title: Latency to your users
items.body: The physical distance between the facility and the people using the service is the single largest factor in response time.

items.title: Data residency
items.body: Where data is stored is a legal question as well as a technical one. Region selection is how you answer it.

items.title: The provider operating the facility
items.body: Each region names the provider that runs the physical site.

items.title: Addressing and connectivity
items.body: IP ranges and the network path are determined by the region the service is deployed into.

faqs.q: Why are some regions missing?
faqs.a: Because the platform is not configured to deploy there. Adding a region is an administrative configuration change, and it appears on this page as soon as it is configured.

faqs.q: Does CloudHost247 own the data centres?
faqs.a: No. The facilities are operated by infrastructure providers. CloudHost247 operates the platform and the services that run on the hardware.

faqs.q: Can I deploy across more than one region?
faqs.a: Yes, where more than one is configured. Multi-region architecture is designed per requirement — talk to us about what you are trying to achieve.

pages.title: Network
pages.description: The CloudHost247 network layer: public and private addressing, firewall filtering, reverse DNS, floating IPs and the observability that sits on top.

hero.heading: The path between your users and your service
hero.lede: Addressing, filtering, routing and the telemetry that tells you what is actually happening on the wire.

items.title: IP addressing
items.body: Public addresses assigned to your service, managed in your account, with the option to move a floating address between servers.

items.title: Reverse DNS
items.body: PTR records set correctly, which matters for mail deliverability and for anything that logs connections.

items.title: Firewall filtering
items.body: Rules applied in order to allow, deny or rate-limit traffic to a server, with the order visible.

items.title: Flood mitigation
items.body: Known-abusive traffic patterns are filtered at the network edge rather than reaching the application.

items.title: Traffic telemetry
items.body: Throughput and packet-level signals recorded per service so a change in behaviour is visible as a graph.

items.title: IPv6
items.body: Dual-stack addressing where the region and provider support it.

sections.heading: Bandwidth and traffic terms are contractual
sections.body: Whether a service is unmetered, capped or burstable depends on the product you have, and the number that matters is the one on the plan you bought — not a figure on a marketing page. Where a fair-use expectation applies, it is written down in the Fair Usage Policy.

faqs.q: Can I get additional IP addresses?
faqs.a: Yes, subject to the region and provider. Addresses are assigned to the service and are visible in your account.

faqs.q: Do you support private networking between servers?
faqs.a: Where the provider and region support private networks, servers can be given private addressing that is not reachable from the internet.

faqs.q: Is there a bandwidth limit?
faqs.a: The limit is the one stated on the product you bought. Anything described as unmetered still operates under the Fair Usage Policy.

pages.title: Operating Systems
pages.seoTitle: Supported Operating Systems for Servers | CloudHost247
pages.description: The operating system catalogue available when provisioning a server on CloudHost247, including version lifecycles and provider image availability.

hero.heading: Choose the base your service runs on
hero.lede: The platform holds images for the operating systems it can provision, tracks their lifecycle status, and shows availability per provider region — so you know what you will actually get.

sections.heading: Facts the platform keeps track of

items.title: Families and versions
items.body: Each entry is a specific family, version and architecture rather than a vague name.

items.title: Lifecycle status
items.body: End-of-life operating systems are marked, because a server installed today should not be unsupported next year.

items.title: Provider image availability
items.body: An operating system is only selectable where the provider in that region actually offers an image for it.

items.title: Control panels
items.body: Where a panel is configured to be provisioned on top of an operating system, that mapping is explicit.

items.title: Administerable
items.body: Versions, images and availability are configuration, maintained by administrators rather than hardcoded in the application.

items.title: Supported means patched
items.body: Operating systems with active vendor security support are the ones worth provisioning; the catalogue shows which those are.

sections.heading: If a version is not in the list, it is not provisionable
sections.body: This catalogue reflects what the platform is configured and able to install. A version that is not listed has no image configured for the selected region — we would rather show a shorter list than accept an order we cannot provision.

faqs.q: Can I install a custom ISO?
faqs.a: Where the provider and region support custom images, yes. Availability depends on the underlying infrastructure provider.

faqs.q: Do you offer Windows Server?
faqs.a: Windows-based services are available as products, and Windows images appear in the catalogue where licensing and the region allow.

faqs.q: How are end-of-life systems handled?
faqs.a: They are marked in the catalogue so you can make an informed choice, and support will tell you if the version you are running has reached end of life.

pages.title: Server Management
pages.description: Server management from CloudHost247: provisioning, operating-system lifecycle, monitoring, firewall control, backups, patching and hands-on administration.

hero.heading: The work between a server and a reliable service
hero.lede: Provisioning is the easy part. Keeping a fleet patched, monitored, backed up and reachable — and knowing when something has drifted — is the job.

sections.heading: What the platform does for you

items.title: Provisioning and rebuilds
items.body: Create servers from a catalogue image, rebuild them from a known-good state, and record which image each server runs.

items.title: Access management
items.body: Administrative access is issued and rotated through the platform, and server credentials are stored encrypted rather than pasted into tickets.

items.title: Monitoring and alerting
items.body: Resource telemetry collected per server, with alerting so a saturation event is noticed while it is still an event.

items.title: Firewall control
items.body: Rules attached to the server, applied in a defined order, with the effective ruleset visible.

items.title: Backups
items.body: Scheduled jobs with a run history and a restore path from your account.

items.title: Reconciliation and logs
items.body: The platform compares desired state with provider reality and records every infrastructure operation for audit.

sections.heading: Hand the platform layer to us

items.label: Patching and hardening
items.body: Operating system and platform components patched on a schedule, with the changes recorded.

items.label: Monitoring response
items.body: Alerts are acted on rather than merely delivered — the difference between monitoring and management.

items.label: Incident handling
items.body: A named path for an incident: who is looking, what is being tried, and what customers are told.

items.label: Change management
items.body: Changes made deliberately, with a way back, instead of directly on production at 17:55 on a Friday.

faqs.q: Can you manage a server you did not provision?
faqs.a: That depends on the provider and the access you can grant. Bring the details and we will confirm what is possible.

faqs.q: What counts as managed?
faqs.a: The platform layer: operating system, runtime, monitoring, backups, firewall and response. Application-level administration and code changes are a separate engagement.

faqs.q: Do you support panels like cPanel or Plesk?
faqs.a: Panels are provisioned where the platform is configured to install them, and the control panels page lists what is available rather than what is theoretically possible.

pages.title: Monitoring
pages.description: Resource monitoring and service telemetry for CloudHost247 servers, applications and hosting, with historical data and alerting you can act on.

hero.heading: Know before your customers do
hero.lede: Telemetry collected from the services you actually run, kept as history, so capacity planning is a data question and an incident has a timeline.
points: Status page driven by real checks

items.title: Compute pressure
items.body: CPU and memory over time, so the difference between a busy day and a capacity problem is visible.

items.title: Storage growth
items.body: Disk consumption trending, because a full disk takes a service down quietly and completely.

items.title: Traffic
items.body: Throughput in and out, which is where a traffic spike or a leak is first detectable.

items.title: Service state
items.body: Whether each service is reachable and answering, recorded as state rather than as a promise.

items.title: Alerts that mean something
items.body: Notifications tied to a threshold rather than to every fluctuation, so an alert is worth reading.

items.title: History
items.body: Retained telemetry you can go back through when working out when a problem actually started.

sections.heading: Why there is no uptime figure on this page
sections.body: A meaningful uptime number has to come from independent, continuous, customer-visible measurement over a defined period. Anything else is a claim. The service status page reports the checks this platform can genuinely perform right now, and says plainly when something is not being monitored.

faqs.q: Can I see monitoring for a service I have?
faqs.a: Yes — telemetry is attached to the service in your account, so the graphs for a given server appear with that server.

faqs.q: Do you alert me or fix it yourself?
faqs.a: Both are possible. Standard monitoring notifies; managed services mean the alert is acted on by us as well.

faqs.q: Can I monitor something outside CloudHost247?
faqs.a: The Tools Center includes network and DNS diagnostics that can check external endpoints from the platform.

pages.title: Server & Cloud Backups
pages.description: Backup jobs for CloudHost247 servers and applications: scheduled runs, visible history, defined retention and restores performed from your account.

hero.heading: Backups your services can be restored from
hero.lede: Scheduled jobs attached to the service they protect, with a run history and a retention period you can see — and a restore you can actually perform.

items.title: Scheduled runs
items.body: Backups happen on a schedule attached to the service, not on someone's memory.

items.title: Scoped per service
items.body: A server, an application and a hosting account each have their own backup record, so one restore never affects another.

items.title: What a backup contains
items.body: Each record states what was captured — files, databases, volumes — so you know what a restore will bring back.

items.title: Separate storage
items.body: Backup data is held on storage separate from the live service, so losing a server does not lose its backups.

items.title: Restore path
items.body: Restores run against the service, with the selected backup shown before the restore begins.

items.title: Failure visibility
items.body: A failed run is recorded as failed, which is the only way to know a backup plan is not quietly doing nothing.

faqs.q: How often do backups run?
faqs.a: The schedule is per service. The job history in your account shows the runs that actually happened, which is more reliable than any statement about intent.

faqs.q: Can I take a backup right now?
faqs.a: Yes. A manual run can be triggered before a change, and it appears in the same history as the scheduled runs.

faqs.q: What is the retention period?
faqs.a: Retention differs by service and is stated in the Backup Policy, which is the authoritative document.

pages.title: Firewalls
pages.description: Rule-based firewall control for CloudHost247 servers: ordered allow, deny and rate-limit rules applied at the network layer, with the effective ruleset visible.

hero.heading: Close everything you do not need
hero.lede: Most exposed servers are exposed because a port was opened for one reason and never closed. Firewall rules make the intended surface explicit and reviewable.

items.title: Ordered evaluation
items.body: Rules are applied in sequence and the order is shown, because order is what determines the outcome.

items.title: Default deny
items.body: A policy of closing everything and opening what the service needs is the one that ages well.

items.title: Rate limiting
items.body: Limit connections from a source so a brute-force attempt or a runaway client cannot consume the service.

items.title: Source restrictions
items.body: Restrict administrative ports to known addresses so SSH is not reachable from the whole internet.

items.title: Per-service rules
items.body: Rules are attached to a specific server, so a change is scoped to the thing it was meant for.

items.title: Auditable changes
items.body: Rule changes are recorded against your account, which makes an incident review possible.

faqs.q: Can I lock myself out?
faqs.a: Yes — that is a real risk with any firewall. Platform-level console access exists for the servers that support it, and support can help recover access.

faqs.q: Is the firewall in front of the server or on it?
faqs.a: Rules are applied at the network layer for the service, ahead of the application, and are managed from the platform rather than requiring you to edit rules on the host.

faqs.q: Does it protect against volumetric attacks?
faqs.a: Network-level flood mitigation is part of the platform, but the capacity available depends on the region and provider. A firewall is a policy control, not a substitute for mitigation capacity.

pages.title: Cloud Security
pages.description: How CloudHost247 secures cloud services: credential handling, isolation, network control, patch management, logging and incident response.

hero.heading: The controls behind the services
hero.lede: Credentials stored rather than pasted, access restricted and recorded, infrastructure patched on a schedule, and every operation logged.

items.title: Provider credentials
items.body: Infrastructure provider credentials are stored encrypted, never returned to a browser, and used only by the platform's own operations.

items.title: Audit trail
items.body: Infrastructure operations and administrative actions are recorded, so who did what and when is answerable.

items.title: Role-based access
items.body: Administrative capability is granted by role and re-verified server-side on every request rather than trusted from the interface.

items.title: Service isolation
items.body: Customer services are separated so that one cannot read or control another.

items.title: Patch management
items.body: Operating systems and platform components are patched on a schedule, with changes tracked against the service.

items.title: Incident response
items.body: A defined path for detection, containment, notification and review — written down before it is needed.

items.label: Turn on multi-factor authentication
items.body: TOTP and passkey authentication are supported. A password alone is the weakest link in any hosting account.

items.label: Review administrative users
items.body: Staff and administrative access should be limited to people who need it, and removed when they do not.

items.label: Keep recovery details current
items.body: Password recovery and second-factor recovery both depend on the contact details on the account being right.

faqs.q: Where are credentials stored?
faqs.a: Provider and server credentials are encrypted at rest and are never included in API responses. Access is limited to the platform operations that need them.

faqs.q: Do you log administrative access?
faqs.a: Yes. Administrative actions and infrastructure operations are written to an audit log in the platform.

faqs.q: Who do I contact about a security issue?
faqs.a: Use the abuse and security route published in the legal and policy documents. Reports are handled under the Cybercrime and Abuse Policy.

pages.title: IP Management
pages.seoTitle: IP Address & Reverse DNS Management | CloudHost247
pages.description: Manage the IP addresses assigned to your CloudHost247 services: public addressing, floating IPs, reverse DNS and the records that tie them to your services.

hero.heading: Know which address belongs to what
hero.lede: Addresses assigned to services, reverse DNS that resolves correctly, and the ability to move an address between servers without asking support.

items.title: See the assignment
items.body: Every address shows the service it belongs to, so an audit does not require a spreadsheet.

items.title: Set reverse DNS
items.body: PTR records for your addresses, which mail servers and log correlation both depend on.

items.title: Move an address
items.body: A floating address can be reassigned to another server, which is what makes failover practical.

items.title: IPv6 where available
items.body: Dual-stack assignment where the region and provider support it.

items.title: Justification for more
items.body: Additional address requests are assessed against real need, which is what keeps the pool usable for everyone.

items.title: Abuse handling
items.body: Addresses reported for abuse are handled under the Acceptable Use Policy, whichever service holds them.

faqs.q: Can I get a dedicated IP for a website?
faqs.a: Where the product supports it and the region has addresses available. Raise the requirement and the option is confirmed with the service.

faqs.q: Why does reverse DNS matter?
faqs.a: A PTR record that matches the sending hostname is a deliverability signal for mail, and it makes connection logs meaningful for everything else.

faqs.q: Do addresses transfer if I move servers?
faqs.a: A floating address can be reassigned within the same region. A change of region means a new address.

pages.title: Website Migration

hero.heading: Move your site without holding your breath
hero.lede: A migration is a sequence of small, reversible steps — copy, verify, then switch. The old host keeps serving until the new one has proved itself.

items.title: Inventory
items.body: We establish what is moving: files, databases, mailboxes, cron jobs, DNS records and any external service the site calls.

items.title: Provision the target
items.body: The destination account or server is created and configured to match the application's requirements before anything is copied.

items.title: Copy the data
items.body: Files and databases are transferred and the application is adjusted for the new path, hostname and connection details.

items.title: Verify on a real hostname
items.body: The copied site is served on a temporary hostname and checked: pages resolve, forms submit, mail authenticates, the certificate is valid.

items.title: Switch DNS
items.body: Only after verification, the domain's records are updated. Because the old host is untouched, this step is reversible.

items.title: Confirm and tidy
items.body: We confirm the live site and mail behave, then the old copies and any temporary hostnames are removed.

sections.heading: What we need from you
sections.body: Access to the current host, the domain's DNS control, and a list of anything the site depends on that is not obvious from the files — third-party APIs, scheduled jobs, unusual mail routing. Migrations go wrong when a dependency is discovered afterwards.

faqs.q: How long does a migration take?
faqs.a: It depends on the size of the data and how the current host allows access. The copy and verification happen before any customer-visible change, and the DNS switch itself is decided by you.

faqs.q: Will my site be down during the move?
faqs.a: The intent of the sequence is no downtime: the site is verified on the new infrastructure while the old one still serves, and DNS is the only change that customers can observe.

faqs.q: Can you migrate email as well as the website?
faqs.a: Yes. Mailboxes and their contents are part of the inventory, and the MX records change at the same carefully chosen moment as the web records.

faqs.q: What if the migration does not work?
faqs.a: Verification happens before the switch, so a failed migration is caught while the original site is still live. If the new platform cannot run the application, you keep the old host and we say so.

sections.heading: Why there is no historical uptime percentage
sections.body: An uptime figure is only meaningful when it comes from continuous, independent, long-term measurement. Publishing a percentage derived from anything else would be a made-up number with a decimal point, which is worse than publishing none.

pages.title: Security & Compliance
pages.description: How CloudHost247 secures its platform and customer data: authentication, access control, encryption, isolation, logging and responsible disclosure.

hero.heading: Security stated as practice, not as decoration
hero.lede: What we actually do to protect accounts, data and infrastructure — and what we deliberately do not claim, because a badge is not a control.
points: Encryption in transit and at rest

items.title: Authentication
items.body: Password hashing with a memory-hard algorithm, multi-factor authentication by TOTP, and passkey (WebAuthn) sign-in as a phishing-resistant option.

items.title: Least privilege
items.body: Role-based access for administrative functions, re-verified server-side on every request rather than trusted from the interface.

items.title: Encryption
items.body: TLS for every public endpoint and mail transport, with certificates issued and renewed automatically; sensitive values encrypted at rest.

items.title: Isolation
items.body: Customer services are separated, and provider credentials are held encrypted and used only by platform operations.

items.title: Logging and audit
items.body: Authentication events, administrative actions and infrastructure operations are recorded, giving an answer to who did what and when.

items.title: Response
items.body: A defined incident path: detection, containment, notification and review — documented before it is needed.

items.label: Tell us, privately
items.body: Report through the contact route with enough detail to reproduce it. Do not test against another customer's service or data.

items.label: We will acknowledge and investigate
items.body: Reports are triaged, and you get a response from a person who can act on it rather than an automated reply.

items.label: Do not access data that is not yours
items.body: Proof of concept that stops at the boundary of your own account is welcome. Going further is not authorised, whatever the intention.

sections.heading: Certifications we do not claim
sections.body: Where a compliance framework matters to you — ISO 27001, SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA — ask, and you will get an accurate answer including 'not certified'. Publishing a certification we do not hold would be the single most damaging thing this page could do.

faqs.q: Do you support two-factor authentication?
faqs.a: Yes — TOTP-based multi-factor authentication and WebAuthn passkeys are both supported on accounts.

faqs.q: How is customer data protected?
faqs.a: Data is isolated per service, encrypted in transit, and access is role-restricted and logged. The Data Protection Standards document describes the controls in more detail.

faqs.q: Where is data stored?
faqs.a: In the regions configured for the services you use. The data centres page lists the regions this deployment can actually deploy into.

faqs.q: Can you complete a security questionnaire?
faqs.a: Yes. Send it through the contact route and you will get answers to the questions that can be answered, and a clear 'not applicable' or 'not held' where that is the truth.
